updateCadence: Rare; fork releases when fixes accumulate
summary: w3m is a terminal browser that renders tables and frames, supports tabs, and can show inline images in capable terminals. Like Lynx it has no JavaScript, and upstream is largely inactive with forks carrying on.
bestFor: Terminal users who want tabs and table rendering
Use as a pager/HTML viewer (mutt, Emacs w3m)
notFor: Users who need an actively maintained, security-audited browser

pros.title: Better layout than Lynx
pros.detail: Renders tables and frames in text, with tabs and mouse support.

pros.title: Inline images
pros.detail: With w3m-img and a suitable terminal it can display images inline.

pros.title: Great as a pager
pros.detail: Pipes HTML or text through it, and integrates with Emacs (emacs-w3m).

cons.title: Upstream inactive
cons.detail: Original project stalled; there are competing forks, so patch speed is uncertain.

cons.title: No JavaScript
cons.detail: Modern sites and logins largely fail.

cons.title: Security history
cons.detail: Memory-safety bugs have been reported in the C code base over the years.

faq.a: The original project is not, but forks exist; Wikipedia lists 0.5.6 as of 2026-01-23 and a SourceHut fork still in development.
Yes in supported terminals, usually via the separate w3m-img package.

timeline.event: Debian-oriented fork by Tatsuya Kinoshita becomes the practical upstream
Kinoshita steps away; new community fork (~rkta/w3m on SourceHut) starts

switching.note: No importers; bookmark file is local.

pageLoad: Fast fetch; tables render, no CSS/JS
graphics: No WebGL or canvas; optional inline images only
blocking: No filter lists; mostly relies on no-JS
securityHardening: No sandbox; C code with a memory-safety bug history
productivity: Pager use, no notes or reader
webCompat: Static HTML, tables and frames only
accessibility: Linear text output; less documented than Lynx

featureNotes.trackingProtection: No JS; cookies can be disabled
